title: Precision Rectifier: 4 Smart Op Amp Designs for Tiny Signals
text:
Analog Electronics

 Precision Rectifier: 4 Smart Op Amp Designs for Tiny Signals

 An ordinary diode ignores anything below about 0.6 V, but place it inside an op amp loop and it rectifies millivolts cleanly.

 
 Superdiode 
 Half Wave 
 Full Wave 
 Absolute Value 
 




 Ordinary diode rectifiers work well for mains voltages but fail on small signals because of their forward drop. An op amp placed around the diode removes that drop and produces an accurate rectified output.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a precision rectifier works, how half wave and full wave op amp circuits are built, and what limits their accuracy at higher frequency.


 
 
 
 What Is a Precision Rectifier?


 A precision rectifier is an op amp circuit that rectifies an AC signal without the forward voltage error of a plain diode, so it can handle signals of only a few millivolts. It is sometimes called a superdiode, and it improves on the diode rectifier circuits used in power supplies.


 CircuitDigest explains that the op amp cancels the usual 0.6 V to 0.7 V drop. That makes the circuit suitable for precision measurement and instrumentation.


 
 
 Image credit: CircuitDigest 
 

 The trick is negative feedback, a core idea from op amp basics . The op amp raises its own output by exactly the diode drop, so the load sees the true input.


 The effective threshold becomes the diode drop divided by the open loop gain. With a gain of 100000, a 0.6 V drop shrinks to about 6 µV.


 4 Smart Precision Rectifier Circuits


 
 Simple Superdiode
 Diode inside a follower loop.
 Best for: low frequency positive half wave
 Basic 

 Improved Half Wave
 Inverting stage with two diodes that keeps the op amp out of saturation.
 Best for: faster, cleaner half wave output
 Popular 

 Full Wave Two Op Amp
 Half wave stage plus a summing amplifier.
 Best for: absolute value and AC meters
 Accurate 

 Single Supply Full Wave
 Uses rail to rail op amps and resistor ratios.
 Best for: battery powered sensors
 Compact 




 The simple superdiode precision rectifier lets the op amp saturate on negative half cycles. It must then slew back from the rail, which distorts fast signals.


 The improved half wave circuit adds a second diode that closes the loop during the other half cycle. The op amp output then only swings about two diode drops.


 How the Improved Half Wave Circuit Works


 
 Negative Input Output goes positive, D1 conducts

 Inverting Gain Output equals minus Rf ÷ Rin times input

 Positive Input Output goes negative, D2 conducts

 Clamp Output held near zero

 Clean Half Wave Only one polarity passes




 TI covers this arrangement in its Analog Engineer circuit note, with design steps for resistor and diode choice. Low leakage, fast switching diodes give the best results.


 Schottky diodes reduce the swing further, as explained in Schottky diode . Check their leakage, which rises with temperature.


 Full Wave Absolute Value Circuit


 
 Half wave stage: V1 = minus Vin for Vin above zero, else 0 
 Summer: Vout = minus (Vin + 2 × V1) 
 Result: Vout = |Vin| 

Example, sine input 100 mV peak:
Average of full wave output = 0.637 × 100 = 63.7 mV
RMS of the sine = 0.707 × 100 = 70.7 mV
 Meter scaling uses form factor 1.11 to read RMS from the average 



 CircuitDigest notes that the full wave version adds a summing amplifier so both half cycles are rectified. Resistor matching of 0.1 percent keeps the two halves equal.


 Average responding meters use this circuit, then scale by 1.11 to show RMS for sine waves. True RMS converters are explained in RMS value .


 Speed and Accuracy Limits


 
 1
 Slew Rate
 Output must jump across the diode drops at each zero crossing.


 2
 Gain Bandwidth
 Loop gain falls at high frequency, raising error.


 3
 Offset Voltage
 Adds directly to small signals.


 4
 Diode Leakage
 Causes error at low levels and high temperature.


 5
 Resistor Matching
 Sets full wave symmetry.





 The crossover dead time is roughly the swing divided by slew rate. A 0.5 V per µs op amp needs about 2.4 µs to swing 1.2 V, which matters at 10 kHz and above.


 Choose a fast op amp with low offset, or add a small offset trim. For a millivolt precision rectifier, offset is often the biggest error.


 Where a Precision Rectifier Helps


 
 AC Voltmeters
 Average responding measurements.


 LVDT Demodulation
 Recovering displacement from AC output.


 Envelope Detection
 Audio and vibration amplitude.


 Peak Detectors
 Capturing maximum values.


 CT Signal Processing
 Measuring small AC currents.


 Level Indicators
 Audio VU meters and alarms.





 An LVDT gives an AC output that must be rectified accurately. Such circuits are part of wider signal conditioning .


 Response Calculator


 
 Output and Crossover Time

 Frequency, kHz

 Swing at crossover, V

 Result

 Keep the crossover share below about 1 percent for good accuracy. Choose a faster op amp or lower the frequency if it is higher.


 
 Advantages

 
 Rectifies millivolt signals.

 Accurate and linear.

 Works with single or dual supplies.

 Easy to scale with resistors.

 
 

 Limitations

 
 Speed limited by slew rate.

 Offset error at low levels.

 Needs matched resistors.

 More parts than a diode alone.

 Precision Rectifier FAQ


 
 What is a precision rectifier?
 An op amp circuit that rectifies without the diode forward drop.


 Why is it called a superdiode?
 It acts like a diode with an almost zero threshold.
